target_customer: College students, reached first through sorority house group drops, who buy clothing
problem: Students want to try clothes at home without shipping hassle or returns friction, and shopping online carries fit risk.
business_model: Free try-at-home e-commerce, customer pays only for items kept, retail margin on curated clothing

founders.name: Harry Berg
founders.background_notes: YC page bio says full stack AI engineer. Education and employers not listed.

founders.name: Holly Leslie
founders.background_notes: YC bio says passionate about making e-commerce delightful. Axios Charlotte (2023) describes the founder as originally from London. Crunchbase snippet lists her as co-founder and CEO.

exit.reason: No shutdown announcement found. CB Insights states the company ceased operation.

technical_complexity.rationale: Curated catalog, logistics and returns handling. Standard e-commerce engineering with the hard part being operations and inventory, not software.

defensibility.rationale: Try-at-home retail was copyable by anyone who could source clothing. Only campus ambassadors and sorority relationships gave some local pull.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source found on incumbent response to Adla specifically.

market_need_then: Students were an under-served shopping segment with limited local retail. Voxburner (trend coverage) and a 2019 Oklahoma State student paper described campus drops across three US colleges. No spend data found.

branding.domain_note: Site tryadla.com now redirects to an unrelated domain (checked 2026-11).
branding.community_and_virality: Local ambassadors named Adla Angelz and sorority house group drops, per a Charlotte article.

brand_strength.rationale: Little press about the brand itself. Student ambassadors called Adla Angelz suggest a campus-community tactic, but no evidence of wide recognition.

outcome_analysis: Adla ran a try-at-home clothing service aimed at college students and reached sorority houses at several campuses, but it never raised beyond a small YC seed that a database reports at 150 thousand dollars. The cause of closure is not public. Free returns and curated inventory are capital intensive, so unit economics and an inability to fund inventory are plausible but unconfirmed, and the factors listed are inferences from the model, not from a source.
notes: The seed round rests on one database (CB Insights). A second CB Insights entity (adla-1) lists a 500K convertible note dated January 2019 from YC, which conflicts and may be a different entity; not recorded as a round. CB founding year 2018 versus YC batch Summer 2019. Dated competitor sources near the batch were not found, so the list is empty. Failure factors are inferred because the cause is not public.
